tip: The plain -ना (naa) verb form works as a gentle command between close people: याद दिला देना (yaad dila dena) = do remind me. Softer than an order, common in families.
को (ko) marks a definite object: बक्से को (bakse ko) means that specific heavy box. Drop को and it reads like some box or other.
को (ko) can single out a specific object: ट्रक को (truck ko) = that particular truck. Drop it and ट्रक रोका (truck roka) reads as stopping some truck, not this one.
You don't 'like' things in Hindi – they strike you as good: अच्छा लगा (achchha laga = felt good) means 'I liked it'. The liker takes मुझे (mujhe = to me).
बड़े दिनों बाद (bade dinon baad) is literally 'after big days' – Hindi's way of saying 'after ages'. बड़ा (bada = big) stretches to mean 'long' with time.
अच्छा (achchha) at the start of speech isn't 'good' – it's 'alright, OK'. अच्छा, फिर मिलते हैं (phir milte hain) = 'alright, see you again'.
Dark colors are deep in Hindi: गहरा नीला (gahra neela = deep blue) is 'dark blue'. Light shades use हल्का (halka = light).
Doubling an adjective adds 'all sorts of': नई-नई किताबें (nayi-nayi kitaben) = various brand-new books. Hindi repeats the word where English reaches for 'all kinds of'.
-ी adjectives never change for number or respect: अच्छी (achchhi = good) fits one woman or many. Only the verb हैं (hain) shows the respect here.
इतना बड़ा (itna bada) is literally 'this much big' – Hindi measures with इतना where English says 'such a'. इतना बड़ा घर (itna bada ghar) = such a big house.
Sizes are possessed: चालीस किलोमीटर की (chalees kilometre ki) = 'of forty kilometers'. The road isn't 40 km long – it's OF 40 km.
मोटा (mota) means thick AND fat: मोटी किताब (moti kitab) = thick book, but said of a person it's 'fat'. English splits the two words, Hindi doesn't.
-ा adjectives agree with gender: पुराना (purana=old, m) but पुरानी गाड़ी (purani, f).
मिलना (milna = to be gotten) does the work of 'find': अस्पताल नहीं मिलता (aspatal nahin milta) = a hospital isn't found. No 'you' in the Hindi at all.
बड़े भाई (bade bhai) is 'elder brother', not a big one – बड़ा (bada) marks age in family words. Younger siblings are छोटा (chhota = small).
Hindi says sour-sweet where English says sweet-sour: खट्टी-मीठी (khatti-mithi). Paired-taste adjectives run in the opposite order.
The superlative is 'from all': सबसे अच्छी (sabse achchhi = good from all) = the best. सब (sab = all) + से (se = from) replaces any '-est' ending.
और (aur) before an adjective means 'even more', not 'and': और अच्छी (aur achchhi) = even better. Placement flips the meaning.
'-er than' is just से (se = from): तुम्हारे कमरे से बड़ा (tumhare kamre se bada) = 'big from your room' = bigger than it. The adjective itself never changes.
'A bit' agrees in Hindi: थोड़ी कड़वी (thodi kadvi = a bit bitter) is feminine to match दवा (dava = medicine). English 'a bit' never changes – थोड़ा does.
One respected man, everything plural: मेरे बहनोई (mere bahnoi), अच्छे (achchhe), हैं (hain) – possessive, adjective and verb all take plural for respect.
Sleep comes to you in Hindi: नींद नहीं आई (neend nahin aayi = sleep didn't come) = I couldn't sleep. You're the destination, not the sleeper.
Things fit by arriving: सामान आ जाएगा (saman aa jayega = the stuff will come) means it will fit. No separate word for 'fit' needed.
General truths take होती है (hoti hai): here अलग होती है (alag hoti hai) = is different, as a rule. Plain है (hai) would mean just right now.
English tea 'has gone' cold; Hindi tea became it: ठंडी हो गई है (thandi ho gayi hai = has become cold). हो जाना (ho jana) covers most changes of state.
Fit points at you: मुझे थोड़े तंग हैं (mujhe thode tang hain) = 'a bit tight TO me'. English says 'for me'; Hindi uses मुझे (mujhe = to me).
Even one office bends the adjective: बड़े दफ्तर में (bade daftar mein = in a big office). Before में, बड़ा (bada) becomes बड़े – no plural involved.
पकौड़े और चाय का मज़ा है (pakaude aur chai ka maza hai) is literally 'is the fun of pakoras and tea' – Hindi names what the delight is OF, with no 'they are'.
से (se = than) makes '-er': मूली से ज़्यादा मीठी (muli se zyada mithi) = sweeter than radish. ज़्यादा (zyada = more) just adds emphasis – Hindi can drop it.
बड़ा (bada) before feelings means 'great', not big: बड़ा शौक (bada shauk) = a strong hobby. Same trick as बड़ी खुशी (badi khushi = great joy).
